ARP Spoofing works by exploiting the stateless nature of the ARP protocol, which does not require authentication. An attacker sends falsified ARP replies to devices on a local network, associating their own MAC address with the IP address of a legitimate device. This causes the victim's devices to update their ARP cache incorrectly, believing they are communicating with the intended device when they are actually communicating with the attacker. The attacker can then eavesdrop on or manipulate the traffic between the victim and the legitimate device, potentially capturing sensitive information such as credentials [Source 2][Source 3].
